q: An impulse reaches a biological neuron from its neighbours. Which part of the neuron receives it first?
options: The axon terminal
A dendrite
The axon
The nucleus
explain: Dendrites receive the impulse from neighbouring neurons. It then passes through the nucleus and the axon and leaves at the axon terminal, which is the exit and not the entry.

q: What does the simplest neural network, a perceptron, consist of?
options: Two hidden layers of neurons feeding one output
Thousands of neurons arranged in many consecutive hidden layers
A single neuron with several input nodes and one output node
One input node connected to several output nodes
explain: In its simplest form a perceptron is one neuron that takes several inputs and gives one output. Thousands of perceptrons arranged in layers make a full network.

q: Each connection leaving an input node of a perceptron has a weight. What does the weight do?
options: It sets how strongly that input counts in the weighted sum
It decides whether the neuron fires for a given weighted sum
It sets how many inputs the neuron has
It measures the error of the final prediction
explain: Inputs are multiplied by their weights and summed, so a larger weight gives that input more influence. The decision to fire belongs to the activation function and not to the weight.

q: In a perceptron, what happens to the weighted sum of the inputs before the activation function sees it?
options: It is squared to measure the error
It is divided by the number of inputs
It is compared with the true label
It has a bias added to it
explain: The perceptron sums the weighted inputs and then adds a bias. Comparing with a label happens in the cost function, outside the neuron.

q: What decision does the activation function of a neuron make?
options: Whether the neuron fires, given its weighted sum
Whether the weights should be updated in this epoch
How far the prediction is from the true label
Which input node has the largest weight
explain: The activation function checks the weighted sum and decides whether the neuron fires. Updating weights is done by backpropagation and gradient descent during training.

q: What kind of output does a step function give for the weighted sum of a neuron?
options: Any real number that grows with the sum
A probability spread across several classes
One of two values, firing or not firing
The error between prediction and label
explain: A step function gives one of two values, 0 or 1, so the neuron either fires or does not. Outputs that grow with the sum or spread across classes belong to other activation functions.

q: Which kind of pattern can a single perceptron learn?
options: Any pattern, given enough epochs
Patterns that are linearly separable
Only patterns with three or more inputs
Patterns that need several hidden layers
explain: A single perceptron can only learn patterns that are linearly separable. Training for more epochs does not remove that limit.

q: A single perceptron fails to learn the XOR function however long it trains. Why?
options: XOR needs more input nodes than a perceptron allows
A step function cannot ever output the value 1
Random initialisation always starts it in the wrong place
The XOR classes cannot be separated by one straight line
explain: XOR cannot be split by one straight boundary, so a single weighted sum and activation cannot separate its classes. Training longer or starting from other random weights does not remove this limit.
flag: The slide only says a single perceptron learns linearly separable patterns. That XOR is not linearly separable is standard textbook knowledge.

q: Which of these happen inside a single perceptron when it produces an output?
options: The prediction error is passed back to earlier layers
Each input is multiplied by its weight and the products are summed
The cost is averaged over the whole training set
A bias is added to the weighted sum
An activation function decides whether the neuron fires
explain: The perceptron sums weighted inputs, adds a bias and applies an activation function. Passing the error backwards and averaging the cost belong to training, not to the neuron's own calculation.

q: Which statements about the weights and biases of a network are correct?
options: They start with random values
They are readjusted using backpropagation and gradient descent
They are fixed by hand before training and never change
Learning means finding values that minimise the error of the output
explain: Weights and biases start random, are adjusted by backpropagation and gradient descent, and learning means finding values that minimise the output error. They are not fixed by hand.

q: Which statements about supervised learning in neural networks are correct?
options: The data carries no labels and the network finds groups on its own
The desired output for each input sample is known in advance
The goal is to learn a function that approximates the relationship between inputs and outputs
A cost function is not needed because the answers are known
Neural networks generally learn in this way
explain: Supervised learning has known desired outputs, aims to learn the input to output relationship, and is how neural networks generally learn. A cost function is still needed to measure how far predictions are from those answers.

q: A network is trained on the iris flower dataset, where each flower has several measurements and a flower type. Which columns are features that the network takes as input?
options: Sepal length
Sepal width
Petal length
Flower type
Petal width
explain: The four measurements form the feature set the network reads. Flower type is the label, which is the answer the network is trained to predict.

q: Right after random initialisation and before any training, what can be said about the predictions of the network?
options: They are close to the labels because the weights start small
They already improve with each forward pass
They are random, because nothing has been optimised yet
They match the labels for the easy classes
explain: Random weights and biases give a random prediction, so garbage in gives garbage out. The labels have not yet been used to adjust anything.

q: Which order describes one round of the training loop, from the first step to the last?
options: Backpropagation, feed forward, gradient descent, cost function
Feed forward, cost function, backpropagation, gradient descent
Cost function, gradient descent, feed forward, backpropagation
Gradient descent, backpropagation, cost function, feed forward
explain: The prediction must exist before its error can be measured, the error must exist before it is sent back, and the derivatives must be known before the weights are updated. The other orders break that chain.

q: Which of these situations allow training to stop?
options: Every weight has become exactly zero
The cost function has converged to a minimum
The network has seen each test sample once
A set maximum number of epochs has been reached
The first forward pass has finished
explain: Training ends when the cost converges to a minimum or a set number of epochs is reached. Zero weights or a single forward pass are not stopping rules.

q: In the training loop, what does the epoch counter count?
options: Each neuron in the hidden layer
Each example in the training dataset
Each value the cost function returns
Each full round of the training loop
explain: The counter goes up once for each full round of the loop, which is forward pass, cost, backpropagation and gradient descent. Training can stop when it reaches a set maximum.
flag: The slide counts each loop round as an epoch. Many textbooks define an epoch as one pass over the training set, so the stem names the loop round.

q: How do a loss function and a cost function usually differ?
options: Loss is for one observation, cost is the average over the training set
Loss is the average over the training set, cost is for one observation
Loss is used for regression, cost is used for classification
Loss is used in testing, cost is used in training
explain: Loss usually describes how well one observation fits, and cost averages that loss across the training set. Reversing the two definitions is a common mistake.

q: What does a cost function return for the predictions of a model on a dataset?
options: A new set of weights for each layer
A label for each unseen sample
One number that measures the prediction error
A list of derivatives for every neuron in the network
explain: A cost function summarises the error between predictions and actual labels as one real number. New weights come from gradient descent, not from the cost function.

q: How does mean squared error treat a prediction that is very far from its target compared with one that is close?
options: It treats both errors as the same size of mistake
It penalises the far prediction much more than the close one
It ignores any error above a fixed threshold
It rewards the far prediction so the model learns faster
explain: Squaring the distance makes far points cost much more than near points. Treating all sizes alike ignores the squaring.
flag: The slide says errors grow exponentially, which is more precisely quadratic growth, so the stem avoids that word.

q: One network predicts house prices and another labels emails as spam or not spam. Which pairing of cost functions fits?
options: Binary cross entropy for the prices and mean squared error for the spam labels
Binary cross entropy for the prices and mean absolute error for the spam labels
Mean absolute error for both the prices and the spam labels
Mean squared error for the prices and binary cross entropy for the spam labels
explain: Prices are continuous values, so a regression cost such as mean squared error fits. Spam or not spam is a target of 0 or 1, so binary cross entropy fits. The other pairings use a regression cost for the spam labels or binary cross entropy for the prices.

q: Which statements about binary cross entropy are correct?
options: It is used when the target is either 0 or 1
It compares the true distribution with the predicted distribution
It measures how far each prediction is from the true value and averages these errors
The prediction is usually produced by a sigmoid or softmax activation
explain: Binary cross entropy suits targets of 0 or 1. It compares the true distribution with the predicted one, averages the error over the predictions, and takes its prediction from a sigmoid or softmax output. All four statements are true.

q: What is gradient descent used for during training?
options: To update the weights and biases so the cost falls
To compute the cost for every sample in the training set
To choose the activation function
To measure performance on unseen data
explain: Gradient descent updates the weights and biases to reduce the cost. The cost function only measures the error, and testing is separate from training.

q: At the current weight, the slope of the cost function is positive. What does this tell gradient descent?
options: Increase the weight, because a positive slope means it is too small
Stop, because a positive slope means the minimum has been reached
Reset the weight to a new random value
Decrease the weight, because moving against the slope lowers the cost
explain: Gradient descent moves in the negative direction of the derivative. With a positive slope that means decreasing the weight, and increasing it would raise the cost.

q: Which statements about backpropagation and gradient descent are correct?
options: Gradient descent produces the forward pass predictions
Backpropagation sends the prediction error back to each layer
Backpropagation measures performance on unseen data
Backpropagation calculates partial derivatives using the chain rule
Gradient descent uses those derivatives to adjust weights and biases
explain: Backpropagation carries the error back and computes partial derivatives with the chain rule, and gradient descent uses them to change weights and biases. The forward pass makes the predictions, and testing uses unseen data.

q: Which statements about testing a trained network are correct?
options: The weights are updated by gradient descent on the test data
It uses new unseen data
Performance is measured on that data
The process is usually called inference
explain: Testing uses new unseen data, measures performance and is usually called inference. The weights are not trained further on the test data.

q: Which statements about a network of perceptrons are correct?
options: The perceptrons work together in consecutive layers
Every perceptron must start with the same weights
The layers turn the input data into predictions based on features present or absent
In the feed forward process information moves from the input layer towards the output layer
A network with layers no longer needs a cost function
explain: Perceptrons work in consecutive layers, turn inputs into predictions based on features, and feed forward moves from input to output. Weights start random and differ, and the cost function is still needed.

q: Explain how an artificial neural network is inspired by the human brain.
model: The brain is a web of interconnected neurons. Each neuron has dendrites that receive impulses from neighbours, a nucleus and a single axon that pass the impulse on, and an axon terminal that releases it to other neurons. Researchers recreated this structure and function with artificial neurons so that a machine could learn, decide and predict in a similar way. An artificial neuron has input nodes in place of dendrites and an output in place of the axon, and many of them are joined into a network.
points: The brain is made of interconnected neurons
Dendrites receive impulses and the axon passes them on
Artificial neurons copy this structure at a small scale
Inputs and outputs of an artificial neuron play the roles of dendrites and axon

q: Describe how a single perceptron turns its inputs into an output.
model: Each input value is multiplied by the weight on its connection. The products are added together to give a weighted sum, and a bias is added to that sum. The result passes to an activation function, which decides whether the neuron fires. With a step function the output is one of two values. The weights and bias start random and are adjusted during training so that the error of the output becomes smaller.
points: Inputs are multiplied by their weights and summed
A bias is added to the sum
An activation function decides whether the neuron fires
Weights and bias are learned to reduce the output error

q: Explain the purpose of an activation function and give one example.
model: An activation function looks at the weighted sum produced by a neuron and decides whether the output connections should fire. The step function is the simplest example, giving one of two values depending on the sum. Sigmoid and softmax are other examples and are often used so that the output of a classification network is a probability. The choice of activation function depends on the task the network has to do.
points: It checks the weighted sum of a neuron
It decides whether the output connections fire
A step function is a valid example
Sigmoid or softmax is a valid example

q: Explain why a single perceptron is limited and how a network of perceptrons goes further.
model: A single perceptron can only learn patterns that are linearly separable, so it cannot solve a problem where one straight boundary cannot split the classes. XOR is a standard example. Placing thousands of perceptrons in consecutive layers lets them work together. Each layer passes its results on, and the network turns the input data into predictions based on the presence or absence of features.
points: A single perceptron only learns linearly separable patterns
Names a problem it cannot learn, such as XOR
A network uses many perceptrons in consecutive layers
Layers turn inputs into predictions based on features
flag: The slides only say a network turns inputs into predictions based on features. The claim that layers overcome the linear limit is standard textbook knowledge.

q: Describe supervised learning using the iris dataset as an example.
model: In supervised learning the correct output for every training sample is known in advance. In the iris dataset each sample has a feature set of sepal length, sepal width, petal length and petal width, and a label giving the flower type. The network takes the features as input and predicts a flower type. The aim is to learn a function that best approximates the relationship between the inputs and the labels so that it can predict well on new samples.
points: Desired outputs are known in advance
Features are the four flower measurements
The label is the flower type
The goal is to learn the input to output relationship

q: Describe the steps of the training loop for a neural network.
model: Training is iterative. First the weights and biases are set randomly. Each round then starts with a forward pass that moves from the input layer to the output layer to give a prediction. The cost function measures the error of that prediction. Backpropagation sends the error back to each layer, and gradient descent adjusts the weights and biases to reduce the error. The epoch counter goes up and the loop repeats until the cost converges or the maximum number of epochs is reached.
points: Random initialisation of weights and biases
Forward pass to make a prediction
Cost function measures the error
Backpropagation and gradient descent update the parameters
Repeat until convergence or the epoch limit

q: Explain why a network gives poor predictions straight after initialisation and what the phrase garbage in garbage out means here.
model: Weights and biases are set randomly across every perceptron, so the first prediction is also random. Nothing has been optimised, and the network has not yet used the labels to learn anything. The phrase garbage in garbage out means that random parameters can only produce meaningless output. Training exists to improve these parameters step by step, so later predictions move closer to the true labels.
points: Weights and biases start random
The first prediction is therefore random
Nothing has been optimised yet
Training improves the parameters over time

q: Compare a loss function with a cost function and give one example of a regression cost and one of a classification cost.
model: A loss function usually refers to the error for one observation, while a cost function usually refers to the average of the loss over the whole training set. Both turn the gap between prediction and true label into a single number that training tries to make small. Mean squared error is a regression example and it punishes distant predictions heavily. Binary cross entropy is a classification example for targets that are either 0 or 1, and it compares the predicted probability with the true label.
points: Loss is for one observation
Cost is the average over the training set
A regression example such as mean squared error
A classification example such as binary cross entropy

q: Explain how gradient descent reduces the cost function.
model: Gradient descent uses the derivative, which is the slope of the cost at the current point. The sign of the slope shows which direction to move. To lower the cost the parameters are moved in the negative direction of the derivative, which is the opposite direction to the gradient. Each corrective update to the weights and biases moves the model towards a better combination of parameters, and repeating the updates drives the cost towards a minimum.
points: It uses the slope of the cost
The sign of the slope gives the direction
Parameters move in the negative direction of the derivative
Repeated updates move the cost towards a minimum

q: Explain how backpropagation and gradient descent work together.
model: Backpropagation sends the prediction error from the cost function back to each layer, and it calculates partial derivatives using the chain rule of calculus. These derivatives show how each weight and bias affects the cost. Gradient descent then uses them to adjust the weights and biases so that the cost is lower in the next round of feed forward, which is the next epoch. So backpropagation finds the direction of improvement and gradient descent makes the change.
points: Backpropagation sends the error back to each layer
It calculates partial derivatives with the chain rule
Gradient descent uses the derivatives to adjust weights and biases
The improvement shows in the next epoch

q: Describe how a trained network is tested.
model: Once training has finished, either because the cost converged to a minimum or because a set number of epochs was reached, the network is tested on new unseen data. The weights are no longer being trained. The network makes predictions and its performance is measured on this data. This process is usually called inference. Testing on unseen data shows how well the learned function works beyond the training samples.
points: Testing follows the end of training
It uses new unseen data
Performance is measured on that data
The process is called inference

q: Explain how an artificial neural network works and how learning takes place during training. Discuss trainable parameters, particularly weights and biases, and their roles in determining the output.
model: An artificial neural network is made of layers of neurons: an input layer, one or more hidden layers and an output layer. Each neuron multiplies its inputs by weights, adds them up with a bias and passes the result through an activation function. The outputs flow forward layer by layer to give a prediction. Training compares the prediction with the true value using a loss function. The error is sent back through the network and the weights and biases are adjusted by backpropagation and gradient descent to reduce it, and this repeats over many examples. Weights and biases are the trainable parameters. A weight sets how strongly an input affects a neuron. A bias shifts the weighted sum so the neuron can activate even when its inputs are zero.
points: Layers of neurons, input, hidden and output
Each neuron takes a weighted sum plus bias and applies an activation function
Training compares predictions with targets using a loss
Weights and biases are adjusted to reduce the loss
Weights set input strength, bias shifts the sum
flag: The mock gives no sample answer. This model answer was written from the slides for that week.

q: Which quantities are typically adjusted during training of a feedforward neural network?
options: Input features and target labels
Weights and biases
Activation function names and dataset size
Number of training observations and output classes
explain: Weights and biases are the trainable parameters. The data and the architecture stay fixed during training.
source: Tutor's mock test, multiple choice question 10

q: What is the main consequence of using only linear activation functions throughout a multilayer feedforward network?
options: The network would automatically become a recurrent model
The network would be unable to represent nonlinear mappings through its stacked layers
The network would no longer require trainable weights
The network would always produce binary outputs
explain: A stack of linear layers collapses into one linear function, so the extra layers add no power to model nonlinear patterns.
source: Tutor's mock test, multiple choice question 11
flag: That stacked linear layers collapse into one linear function is standard textbook reasoning.
